canonicalExplanation.summary: A **header** (`.h`) is a promise: it **declares** what exists (function prototypes, types, macros) so other files can use it correctly. The **definition** (the function body) lives in **exactly one** `.c` file. `#include <stdio.h>` gives you `printf`'s declaration; the C library supplies the definition at link time. Your own headers work the same way. Include the right header for everything you call: without a declaration, the compiler can't check arguments and may reject the call or get it wrong. And including a header **doesn't link** anything by itself; the defining `.c` file or library must still be in the build.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes a `total` function in totals.c, then calls it from main.c and report.c by copying the function into each file. The build fails with `multiple definition of 'total'`. A project header declares int total(const int *values, size_t count) and each caller includes it while one .c file defines the function. In this lesson you'll select required headers and explain the danger of missing or incompatible declarations.

```predict
{"question": "Does `#include \"totals.h\"` make total's code part of your program?", "options": ["Yes, including it adds the code", "No: it only declares total; totals.c must still be compiled and linked"], "answer": 1, "why": "Headers promise; source files and libraries deliver."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Source-to-execution models**, **Editor and terminal workflow** and **Translation unit and main** (what one .c file contains).

sections.heading: The model: declare in headers, define once
Missing declarations

includes: Put declarations, types and macros in headers with include guards, and one definition in a .c file.
Include the header for every function you call, and link the defining file or library.
excludes: Static libraries and linker flags in depth.

outcomes: Select required headers and explain the danger of missing or incompatible declarations.

examples.title: One declaration, one definition
examples.situation: A project header declares int total(const int *values, size_t count) and each caller includes it while one .c file defines the function.
walkthrough: **A project header declares int total(const int *values, size_t count):** totals.h holds the prototype with an include guard.
**Each caller includes it:** main.c and report.c both #include "totals.h" and call total.
**One .c file defines the function:** only totals.c has the body; gcc main.c report.c totals.c will link cleanly.
examples.result: No duplicate definitions, and every call is checked against one prototype.

examples.title: The mismatched prototype
examples.situation: A caller declares `int total(int *values, int count);` by hand instead of including totals.h, and passes a size_t count on a 64-bit system.
walkthrough: The caller's declaration disagrees with the definition: that's undefined behaviour.
The compiler can't catch it, because each file compiled separately with a different promise.
Delete the hand-written declaration and include totals.h everywhere, including totals.c.
examples.result: Every file sees the same declaration, so the compiler checks every call.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Including a header automatically links a library implementation and makes every declared function definition available.
misconceptions.correction: A header only declares. The definition must come from a compiled .c file or a library supplied at link time, or the linker reports undefined references.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what did #include "totals.h" actually provide?

analogy.example: A header is like **a restaurant menu**: it promises dishes and describes them (declarations). The kitchen (one .c file or a library) actually cooks them. Handing out menus in every room doesn't create a kitchen, and two kitchens cooking the same dish for the same order causes chaos (multiple definitions).
limitations: Menus can be vague; prototypes must match exactly.
The C library is a kitchen shared by every program.

steps.explanation: A project header declares the function once.
Each caller includes it, so every call is checked.
One .c file defines the function, and the linker finds it.

nearTransfer.prompt: For each call, name the header: printf, malloc, strlen, sqrt, bool, size_t, EXIT_SUCCESS. Then write a tiny program using three of them with correct includes and a clean -Wall build.
scaffold: stdio.h, stdlib.h, string.h, math.h, stdbool.h, stddef.h.

farTransfer.prompt: Split a single-file program into a header, a definition file and two callers. Add include guards, build all together, then deliberately define a function in the header and show the multiple-definition error when two files include it.
scaffold: Include the header in its own .c file too.
Explain why the error happens at link time.

remediation.explanation: For each function ask: **where is it declared (which header), and where is it defined (which .c file or library)?** Both answers must exist exactly once.

recap.summary: To select headers correctly, include the header that declares every function, type and macro you use, keep your own declarations in guarded headers included by callers and by the defining file, put each definition in exactly one .c file, and remember including a header doesn't link its implementation.
